words.context: A greeting, not a question about your health. The answer is “Yeah, you?” — never an actual status report.
Thanks, in most casual settings. “Ta” is the shorter version and slightly more northern.
Said to people you will not see later. “Cheers” and “bye then” do the same job.
Works for apologising and for getting past. Often said by the person who was bumped into: a reflex, not an admission.
At a bar it’s eye contact and patience. Waving, clicking, or calling out gets you served last.
Asking for “the check” marks you in one syllable.
Usually 12.5%, already on the bill, and removable if you ask. Tipping on top means tipping twice.
Tap your own bank card or phone. Buying an Oyster card is unnecessary, and daily caps apply either way.
Signs say “Toilets.” “Restroom” and “bathroom” both get a blank look, and “washroom” is Canadian.

words.groupNote: “Gents” and “Ladies” on most doors. Pubs occasionally get creative, which is its own small hazard.

words.context: Nobody says “ATM.” Avoid the ones charging a fee — the bank-branded machines are free.
Tap for almost everything, including buses, which take no cash at all.
Increasingly rare. Plenty of places, and every London bus, refuse it outright.
Bags are charged. The sturdy reusable one is called a “bag for life” and gets replaced free when it wears out.
Unnecessary fuss and bother. “It’s a bit of a faff” means it’s technically possible and not worth doing.
Done, arranged, fine. A complete and sufficient answer to almost any question about a plan.
Small, indulgent, technically unearned. “A cheeky pint” is one you weren’t supposed to be having.
Mediocre. British understatement inverts the intensifier: “not bad” is high praise, “quite good” is faint.
The Underground. Never “the subway,” which here means a pedestrian tunnel under a road.
London is priced in concentric zones. Everyone knows their number, and it quietly functions as a class marker.
A plain fry-up café: formica tables, tea in mugs, no concessions to anything. Disappearing, and mourned.
The Tube announcement, now a civic catchphrase. Also the only instruction in London that everyone actually obeys.
